description:
What this operation is trying to become, written down and given a version number. Vision, mission, the SWOT, Porter's five forces, the grand strategy and the exit — the whole apparatus, one record per plan per crop.

PLANS ARE SUPERSEDED, NEVER EDITED INTO THE NEXT ONE. `previous_version` points back at the plan this one replaced and `status` moves to Historical rather than the row being overwritten, because the interesting question about a strategy is almost always what it USED to say. A farm that changed its mind about a market in 2025 needs the 2024 wording to understand why it did.

THE ANALYSIS BLOCKS ARE LONG TEXT AND NOT CHILD TABLES, and that is a considered choice rather than laziness. A SWOT is four lists of sentences somebody wrote in a room; forcing it into rows adds a schema and takes away the sentences. Nothing in this app computes on them — they are read by people — and the moment something does, it will want a shape this doctype cannot guess now.

OBJECTIVES ARE A SEPARATE DOCTYPE, not a child table. See Strategic Objective for why: they are updated on their own cadence by people who are not editing the plan.

fields.description: The crop this plan is for. Empty means farm-wide, which is the usual case for the first plan an operation writes.
fields.label: Crop

fields.description: `Developed` means written and agreed; `Implemented` means somebody is actually running it. The distinction matters because a plan that never left Developed is the most common outcome and the register should say so.
fields.label: Status

fields.description: The span this plan covers, in whatever words the operation uses — '2026-2031', 'through the replant', 'five years'.
fields.label: Timeframe

fields.description: One higher than the plan this one supersedes. Read-only: derived from previous_version on save, because a version number somebody types will eventually be typed twice.
fields.label: Version

fields.description: The plan this one replaces. Self-referential; a chain of these is the operation's strategic history and is the reason nothing here is edited in place.
fields.label: Previous Version

fields.description: When this plan stopped being the live one. Set when a successor is written; a Historical plan with no retired date is a gap in the chain.
fields.label: Retired On

fields.description: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. Free text or JSON — nothing computes on it. See the doctype description.
fields.label: SWOT

fields.description: Threat of new entrants, supplier power, buyer power, threat of substitutes, rivalry among existing competitors.
fields.label: Porter's Five Forces

fields.description: Core competencies and the value-chain reading behind them — what this operation does that is genuinely hard to copy.
fields.label: Sustainable Advantage

fields.description: The game-theory framing: which game this market most resembles and what that implies about how a competitor will respond. Kept because it is the part of a plan people actually reason with.
fields.label: Analogous Games

fields.description: The overall posture — growth, stability, retrenchment, harvest.
fields.label: Grand Strategy

fields.description: How this operation intends to win in its segment: cost, differentiation, focus.
fields.label: Business Strategy

fields.description: Who decides what, and how. Written down because on a farm this is usually understood and never stated, and the first succession event is a bad time to discover the two differ.
fields.label: Command Structure

fields.description: What each function actually does about the strategy — operations, labour, sales, capital.
fields.label: Functional Tactics

fields.description: How anybody would know whether this is working: the KPIs and how they are watched. A strategy with no validation section is a wish.
fields.label: Validation and Control

fields.description: Succession, sale, wind-down. On a family farm this is the hardest section to write and the most expensive one to leave blank.
fields.label: Exit Strategy

name: Strategic Plan
